ocar.opportunity: Three-dimensional electron microscopy can map cells and synapses through large volumes, but heterogeneous samples such as whole insect heads stain poorly with existing en-bloc protocols and their hard cuticle chips during serial cutting.
ocar.challenge: Standard TEM staining was designed for post-section contrast, and widely used FIB-SEM and SBF-SEM protocols work well only on homogeneous tissue pieces, so whole heads do not stain uniformly.
ocar.action: Polilov, Makarova, Pang, Xu, and Hess, in Scientific Reports (2021), tested combinations of fixation, staining, dehydration, and infiltration on whole insect heads using only standard EM reagents and equipment, then imaged with FIB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: The resulting protocol produced FIB-SEM series through a whole head of the parasitoid wasp Megaphragma amalphitanum, with usable contrast in peripheral and central neuropil, compound eye, muscle, and fat body. It was also tested on featherwing beetles and Drosophila melanogaster.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the protocol as enabling whole-head or whole-body ultrastructure for connectomics of receptors, central neuropil, and effector pathways; how well it generalizes beyond the tested insects is left as an application rather than a quantified claim.

summaries.beginner: Insect heads mix hard cuticle, brain, eye, and muscle, so they are hard to stain and cut for 3D electron microscopy. This team reports a lab-friendly preparation that lets them image a whole tiny wasp head at cellular and synaptic detail.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Scientific Reports (2021), Polilov and colleagues describe a sample-preparation protocol for heterogeneous biological material aimed at 3D-EM. Classical TEM stains and existing FIB-SEM/SBF-SEM recipes fail on whole insect heads because cuticle chips and reagents penetrate dissimilar tissues unevenly. Combined with FIB-SEM, the protocol yielded a complete head series of Megaphragma amalphitanum and was also tested on Nephanes titan and Drosophila melanogaster. The authors emphasize that it uses standard EM equipment and reagents rather than specialized connectomics pipelines.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods paper: success is shown as representative sections (brain, eye, muscle, fat body), not as a reconstructed connectome or synapse-detection accuracy. The extract’s conclusions do not quantify staining uniformity, imaging time, or reconstruction completeness. Applicability is claimed for FIB-SEM, SBF-SEM, and TEM without post-section staining; only FIB-SEM of whole heads is illustrated here. Species coverage is three insects, with Megaphragma as the main model.

plain_language_summary: Insect heads mix hard cuticle, brain, eye, and muscle, so they are hard to stain and cut for 3D electron microscopy. This team reports a lab-friendly preparation that lets them image a whole tiny wasp head at cellular and synaptic detail.

ocar.opportunity: Primate broad thorny retinal ganglion cells are highly sensitive to small moving stimuli, but the synaptic circuits that build that motion sensitivity are not well mapped.
ocar.challenge: Their dendrites occupy three contiguous inner-plexiform strata, so both ON and OFF inputs are possible, and it is unclear how much excitation comes from bipolar cells versus amacrine cells.
ocar.action: Bordt, Patterson, and colleagues, in the Journal of Comparative Neurology (2021), reconstructed a broad thorny cell and its presynaptic partners from a serial block-face SEM connectome of central macaque retina, and Puller performed supporting physiology in vitro.
ocar.resolution: Fewer than 2% of inputs were from ON and OFF bipolar cells; the vast majority were from amacrine cells, of which seven morphological types were identified. Physiology confirmed robust excitatory input from both ON and OFF pathways. Identified amacrine cells provided at most six synapses each to this ganglion cell, which received over 1000 amacrine synapses in total.
ocar.future_work: The authors infer that much of the excitatory drive is amacrine-derived and that the same amacrine ensemble likely serves many motion-sensitive ganglion cells; they also predict relatively slow axonal conduction from the cell’s narrow axon diameter.

summaries.beginner: A motion-sensitive cell in the monkey retina gets almost none of its synapses from the usual excitatory bipolar cells. Most of its contacts come from many kinds of amacrine cells, which may help it notice small moving things.
summaries.intermediate: Published in the Journal of Comparative Neurology (2021), Bordt and colleagues analyzed synaptic inputs to a reconstructed broad thorny ganglion cell in a central macaque serial block-face SEM volume. Bipolar cells supplied fewer than 2% of synapses; seven amacrine types (narrow-field knotty bistratified Type 1 and wavy multistratified Type 2; medium-field ON starburst and spiny; wide-field wiry Type 2, stellate wavy, and semilunar Type 2) supplied the rest. In vitro physiology confirmed ON and OFF excitatory input. Identified amacrine cells each contributed at most six synapses to this cell, which received over 1000 amacrine synapses overall.
summaries.advanced: The anatomical sample is one reconstructed ganglion cell (cell 103) whose dendrites reached the volume boundary, so input census is incomplete. “Fewer than 2% bipolar” is reported for this cell, not a population mean. Physiology shows ON/OFF excitation but does not, in this extract, quantify how much of that excitation is bipolar versus amacrine. The seven identified types do not account for all amacrine synapses. Annotations used Viking; the volume is available read-only.

plain_language_summary: A motion-sensitive cell in the monkey retina gets almost none of its synapses from the usual excitatory bipolar cells. Most of its contacts come from many kinds of amacrine cells, which may help it notice small moving things.

ocar.opportunity: Many transcription factors are expressed in scattered neuron types, so studying them in one cell class can miss circuit-level roles. A whole-animal view of C. elegans identity genes can test whether shared regulators also assemble those neurons into a network.
ocar.challenge: unc-42 is expressed in 15 sensory, inter-, and motor neuron classes; whether it only sets each cell’s identity or also wires them together is not obvious from single-cell genetics.
ocar.action: Berghoff, Glenwinkel, Bhattacharya, Hobert, and colleagues, in eLife (2021), mapped unc-42 expression, scored neurotransmitter, receptor, neuropeptide, pathfinding, and synapse phenotypes in mutants, and compared collaborating terminal selectors across those 15 classes.
ocar.resolution: All 15 unc-42(+) classes are synaptically interconnected. unc-42 controls communication-route genes and is required for axon pathfinding and synaptic connectivity, acting as a terminal selector rather than for neuron generation. Mutant locomotion phenocopies surgical removal of unc-42(+) neurons. The authors propose that such factors can serve as circuit-organizer transcription factors.
ocar.future_work: They identify additional transcription factors expressed in synaptically connected neurons and hypothesize that these organizational properties may reflect ontogenetic and phylogenetic trajectories of circuit establishment; that claim is interpretive, not a phylogenetic reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: A single gene in the worm is on in 15 neuron types that all connect to each other. When the gene is missing, those cells fail to take on their adult identities and their wiring goes wrong, so the gene looks like a circuit-building switch.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2021), Berghoff and colleagues show that the C. elegans Prop1-like homeobox gene unc-42 is expressed in 15 synaptically interconnected neuron classes. Mutants disrupt neurotransmitter pathway genes, receptors, neuropeptides, axon pathfinding, and synaptic connectivity, while neuron generation and pan-neuronal features are spared. Continuous larval and adult expression suggests a maintenance role as well. The discussion frames UNC-42 as a terminal selector that collaborates with different co-factors (unc-3, ceh-24, lim-4, fax-1) in different cells, and proposes a broader class of circuit-organizer transcription factors.
summaries.advanced: Penetrance and expressivity of marker loss vary by target gene and cell, and mild unc-42 single-mutant effects can be enhanced by removing a co-terminal selector, so “terminal selector” is not an all-or-none claim. Binding-site analysis is used to predict direct regulation. The 15/118 class count and interconnectivity are the paper’s framing; the extract does not tabulate a full synapse census. Phylogenetic interpretation is hypothesis, not evidence from this study.

plain_language_summary: A single gene in the worm is on in 15 neuron types that all connect to each other. When the gene is missing, those cells fail to take on their adult identities and their wiring goes wrong, so the gene looks like a circuit-building switch.

ocar.opportunity: Large-volume EM connectomes map synapses but usually lack a readout of which synapses were active in vivo, limiting functional interpretation of the wiring diagram.
ocar.challenge: Activity reporters that survive EM processing have mostly been used in culture or acute slices, and serial-section TEM volumes are too small and too thick for accurate vesicle classification across many terminals.
ocar.action: Simon, Roth, Sheridan, Funke, Staras, Häusser, and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2021), combine in vivo FM1-43FX labeling, DAB photoconversion, FIB-SEM, and machine-learning segmentation of photoconverted versus non-photoconverted vesicles in mouse primary visual cortex of awake head-fixed mice.
ocar.resolution: The method yields near-isotropic 3D maps of activated vesicle pools across many synapses. Recycling and non-recycling vesicle counts approximated a lognormal distribution. Neighbouring boutons of the same axon, sharing spike history, could differ greatly in inferred presynaptic release probability.
ocar.future_work: The authors position the approach as opening detailed functional connectomics; how far the vesicle-pool statistics generalize beyond the imaged visual-cortex volume is not established in this extract.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope maps of brain wiring usually cannot say which synapses were firing. This team stains recently used vesicles in living mice, then images them in 3D EM, and finds that even boutons on the same axon can release very differently.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Simon and colleagues combine in vivo FM1-43FX labeling and DAB photoconversion with FIB-SEM and learned vesicle segmentation. In primary visual cortex of awake head-fixed mice they obtain near-isotropic readouts of recycling (photoconverted) versus resting vesicle pools. Pool sizes across synapses approximated a lognormal distribution, and neighbouring boutons of one axon could differ strongly in inferred release probability despite shared spikes. Vesicles within 0.8 µm of a bouton’s largest active zone were assigned to that bouton.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF text captures abstract, introduction, and methods more than a quantitative results narrative, so lognormal fits and bouton-to-bouton Pr differences should be checked against figures not fully present here. Detection used a trained three-class network plus Hough-style post-processing with an empirical score threshold (≥20 on validation data). The study is mouse V1, not a whole-brain functional connectome. “Release probability” is inferred from recycling versus total vesicle pools, not from paired physiology.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope maps of brain wiring usually cannot say which synapses were firing. This team stains recently used vesicles in living mice, then images them in 3D EM, and finds that even boutons on the same axon can release very differently.

ocar.opportunity: A proposed “Mind of a Mouse” project would map a mammalian brain to synapses at a scale compared to the Human Genome Project, raising the question of how industrial-scale neuroscience should be organized.
ocar.challenge: The effort is estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars and about a million terabytes, each mouse brain is unique unlike C. elegans, and it is unclear what such a resource is good for and whether it is worth the cost.
ocar.action: Chen and Flint, in a PLoS Genetics opinion (2021), draw parallels with the Human Genome Project and offer advice from genomics: build resources that working biologists can use immediately, in collaboration with people who already have circuit- and behavior-level questions.
ocar.resolution: They argue that deferred gratification until a whole-mouse map exists may be counterproductive, citing fly-connectome payoffs such as the internal compass from incomplete components. Cartography is valuable, but looking without questions will not suggest mechanism; genetics remains needed to dissect what circuits do.
ocar.future_work: They leave open whether the right goal is a technology project that puts connectomics within reach of a single laboratory, versus committing early to a whole mouse once visual cortex or amygdala exist.

summaries.beginner: A huge project has been proposed to map every synapse in a mouse brain, like sequencing the human genome. This commentary says the map will help most if it is built with biologists who already have questions about circuits and behavior, not as a map for its own sake.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Genetics (2021), Chen and Flint compare the Cell “Mind of a Mouse” proposal to the Human Genome Project: model-organism proofs of principle, technology development, computational centrality, and the need for community buy-in. They note the quoted scale of roughly 1 million terabytes and hundreds of millions of dollars, and that unlike the worm each mouse brain is unique. Their advice is to collaborate with scientists who want to know what a circuit does, to harvest incomplete volumes (as with the fly compass), and to treat genetics as the tool for mechanism once maps exist.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion, not new data. Cost and data-volume figures are quoted from the cited Cell paper, not independently derived. The C. elegans “identical connections” framing is a simplification relative to later variability studies. Recommendations (collaborate early; do not wait for a whole mouse) are policy arguments. No connectome results are reported.

plain_language_summary: A huge project has been proposed to map every synapse in a mouse brain, like sequencing the human genome. This commentary says the map will help most if it is built with biologists who already have questions about circuits and behavior, not as a map for its own sake.

ocar.opportunity: Primate intrinsically photosensitive ganglion cells (ipRGCs) have a rare blue-OFF response whose S-cone circuit was unknown, even though short-wavelength light strongly affects human circadian and other non-image-forming functions.
ocar.challenge: Melanopsin explains much of rodent ipRGC behavior, but the primate blue-OFF pathway required an unidentified inhibitory S-cone interneuron if it is inverted from the S-ON bipolar pathway.
ocar.action: Patterson, Kuchenbecker, Anderson, Neitz, and Neitz, in Current Biology (2020), reconstructed the macaque blue-cone connectome with serial EM and identified an amacrine cell that receives excitatory input exclusively from S-ON bipolar cells and makes selective inhibitory synapses onto ipRGCs.
ocar.resolution: This S-cone amacrine cell supplies the missing inhibitory link that can generate ipRGC blue-OFF responses. The authors interpret it as part of an evolutionarily ancient spectral circuit for non-image-forming vision, well suited to encode sunrise/sunset S versus L/M contrast rather than hue perception.
ocar.future_work: Downstream M1 ipRGC functions are comparatively well known, so the cell can be placed in a named circuit; whether the same motif exists in human retina is implied by primate homology, not shown here.

summaries.beginner: Some ganglion cells that set our body clock also respond to blue light in a special OFF way in primates. This paper finds a new inhibitory cell in the monkey retina that is wired only to blue-sensitive cones and can create that blue-OFF signal.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Biology (2020), Patterson and colleagues reconstructed the S-cone connectome in macaque retina with serial EM. They report an amacrine cell that receives glutamatergic input exclusively from S-ON bipolar cells and makes highly selective inhibitory synapses onto ipRGCs, offering a circuit for the primate blue-OFF response. Discussion places the cell in a conserved S-ON bipolar pathway extended into the inner retina for non-image-forming vision, predicting an S-ON/LM-OFF color-opponent output useful for encoding sky color at sunrise and sunset. Tissue was from a terminally anesthetized male Macaca nemestrina.
summaries.advanced: Anatomical selectivity (exclusive S-ON bipolar input; selective ipRGC output) is the main result; the extract does not report a new physiology experiment that directly records the amacrine cell. Blue-OFF as a consequence is the stated circuit logic, building on prior ipRGC physiology. A UW provisional patent on stimulating circadian rhythms is disclosed. Sample is one animal’s serial EM volume. “Evolutionarily ancient” is an interpretive frame, not a comparative reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Some ganglion cells that set our body clock also respond to blue light in a special OFF way in primates. This paper finds a new inhibitory cell in the monkey retina that is wired only to blue-sensitive cones and can create that blue-OFF signal.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has a complete synaptic wiring list, but the nerve ring was still treated as a packed axon tract, and small reconstruction samples left invariance versus variability unresolved.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic maps alone do not locate physical adjacencies or show how morphology, proximity, and synapses jointly constrain computation.
ocar.action: Brittin, Cook, Hall, Emmons, and Cohen, on bioRxiv (2020), integrate volumetric reconstructions of two nerve rings (young adult and L4) from legacy EM with chemical-synapse and gap-junction connectomes.
ocar.resolution: They report five functional axon bundles that spatially constrain synapses; a stereotyped core circuit embedded in variable background connectivity, for which they propose a reference connectome; and a four-layer Residual Network architecture in which a residual/feed-forward motif accounts for 77% of C4 synapses, with 4% intra-bundle feedback. Architecture is described as supporting sensory computation, sensory-motor convergence, and brain-wide coordination.
ocar.future_work: They suggest these modular, residual features are likely universal across phyla; that is a comparative claim not tested outside C. elegans here.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s brain was long treated as a tangle of axons with a fixed wiring diagram. By rebuilding two nerve rings in 3D, this team finds five bundles, a stable core plus variable extra connections, and a layered layout that looks a bit like a residual neural network.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), Brittin and colleagues present complete volumetric reconstructions of the C. elegans nerve ring from two animals (young adult and L4), spanning about 36 µm, integrated with synaptic and gap-junction connectomes. They describe five functional bundles, argue the connectome is not invariant, and propose a core reference wiring. A four-layer map is compared to a Residual Network: residual connectivity spanning 77% of C4 synapses, plus 4% intra-bundle feedback, with layer 3 as a recurrent trans-bundle circuit. Figure 4 overlays 82 bilateral pairs and 8 single neurons with reproducible nerve-ring synapses.
summaries.advanced: n = 2 animals, so “core versus variable” depends on how reproducibility is thresholded between those two series. “Residual Network” is an analogy to a machine-learning architecture, not a trained model. Universality across phyla is stated as a pointer, not a demonstration. Neighbor definition (physical adjacency in at least one EM section) affects bundle membership. Gap junctions and chemical synapses are both used; the extract does not separate their contributions numerically beyond the 77%/4% figures for the C4 residual map.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s brain was long treated as a tangle of axons with a fixed wiring diagram. By rebuilding two nerve rings in 3D, this team finds five bundles, a stable core plus variable extra connections, and a layered layout that looks a bit like a residual neural network.

ocar.opportunity: Human high-acuity vision depends on a foveal “private-line” from one cone to a midget bipolar to a midget ganglion cell, but it was unknown whether that one-to-one wiring is specified early or sculpted over fetal life.
ocar.challenge: Adult maps cannot distinguish early precise synaptogenesis from later remodeling, and fetal human foveal tissue is rarely available for serial EM.
ocar.action: Zhang, Kim, Dacey, Wong, and colleagues, in Neuron (2020), reconstructed midget circuitry in fetal and adult human fovea by serial electron microscopy at fetal weeks 14 and 18 and in adult tissue.
ocar.resolution: Midget cell types are recognizable by Fwk 14, but cones and midget bipolars initially connect diffusely. By Fwk 18, midget bipolars receive all or nearly all photoreceptor input from a single cone and send most output to single midget ganglion cells. Bipolar–ganglion refinement is more protracted. Cell death between Fwks 14 and 18 likely contributes, and decreasing ribbon densities implicate synapse elimination. Adult private-line at the bipolar–ganglion synapse is still imperfect.
ocar.future_work: The authors cannot rule out later dendritic expansion of narrow-field cells or pruning of wide-field cells, which would increase estimated synaptic divergence.

summaries.beginner: The sharpest part of human vision uses a private line from one cone to one bipolar cell to one ganglion cell. Serial EM of fetal foveas shows that this wiring is carved by remodeling, not born perfect.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Neuron (2020), Zhang and colleagues used serial EM to reconstruct the developing human foveal midget pathway. At fetal week 14, cones contact more than one midget bipolar and vice versa, with substantial bipolar–ganglion convergence and divergence. By fetal week 18, midget bipolars are largely private to one cone and mostly target one midget ganglion cell, while bipolar–ganglion connectivity continues to refine. Adult reconstructions are broadly consistent with prior human and macaque work but still show departures from a pure private line at the bipolar–ganglion synapse. ON and OFF midget bipolar contacts with cones refine faster than those with ganglion cells.
summaries.advanced: Sample is fetal and adult human foveal volumes; exact n of reconstructed cells is not stated in this extract. “Private-line” is a majority, not absolute, adult pattern. Cell death is inferred as a contributor, not isolated experimentally. Narrow-field cells are presumed midgets; later arbor growth could change divergence estimates. Catalog metadata tag the organism as mouse, but the paper is human fovea.

plain_language_summary: The sharpest part of human vision uses a private line from one cone to one bipolar cell to one ganglion cell. Serial EM of fetal foveas shows that this wiring is carved by remodeling, not born perfect.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes invite structure–function mapping, but standard graph metrics may not predict how spiking networks respond to stimuli.
ocar.challenge: Architectural and functional similarity are different metrics, and combinatorial network space makes it unclear which wiring features actually govern population spike patterns.
ocar.action: Haber and Schneidman, on bioRxiv (2020), simulate networks, quantify functional similarity as similitude of spike patterns to the same stimuli, learn a structural metric from synaptic differences, and identify sparse architectural features that predict that similarity.
ocar.resolution: Common graph-theory metrics conveyed little information about response similarity. A learned metric from synaptic differences predicted similarity of held-out networks across a wide stimulus range. The sum of synaptic inputs and of synaptic outputs per neuron predicted functional similarity for networks of up to 100 cells. The authors relate this to homeostatic weight redistribution and “neutral evolution” along manifolds of constant in/out sums.
ocar.future_work: They flag extensions to heterogeneous stimuli, higher-order input correlations, joint stimulus–architecture metrics, pathological silence/epilepsy regimes, and going beyond pairwise synapse differences to loops and global structure.

summaries.beginner: Two brain-like networks can look different as graphs but fire the same way. This simulation study finds that matching each cell’s total incoming and outgoing synapse strength predicts similar activity better than usual network scores.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), Haber and Schneidman measure functional similarity of simulated spiking networks as the similitude of population spike patterns to shared stimuli. Graph-theory metrics performed poorly. A learned metric on synaptic differences predicted similarity of novel networks across stimulus conditions. A sparse feature set—per-neuron summed synaptic input and summed synaptic output—predicted similarity for networks up to 100 cells. Discussion interprets constant in/out sums as manifolds allowing structural change without functional change, consistent with synaptic homeostasis.
summaries.advanced: These are simulated networks, not reconstructed connectomes. Stimulus statistics were homogeneous across neurons; the authors say arbitrary per-cell rates or higher-order input correlations would need a joint metric. The metric is approximately translation-invariant in synaptic-difference space, which they note is unlikely to hold for large differences. Residual unexplained similarity would require beyond-pairwise structure. Pathological (silent or epileptic) regimes were excluded from the main analysis.

plain_language_summary: Two brain-like networks can look different as graphs but fire the same way. This simulation study finds that matching each cell’s total incoming and outgoing synapse strength predicts similar activity better than usual network scores.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse brain connectivity has mostly been analyzed on coarse regional parcels, which can hide continuous, voxel-scale network features.
ocar.challenge: Predefined meta-areas impose sharp borders, bias metrics toward large regions, and may miss directional hub structure and cortical gradients known from primates.
ocar.action: Coletta, Pagani, Whitesell, Harris, Bernhardt, and Gozzi, in Science Advances (2020), analyze the directed mouse connectome at voxel resolution without regional partitioning, relating structure to resting-state fMRI.
ocar.resolution: Integrative hubs segregate into neural sinks and sources along a hierarchical axis. Structural communities spatially reconstitute previously described mouse fMRI networks. Neuromodulatory nuclei appear as connector hubs and orchestrators of inter-modular communication. Cortex is organized along superimposed unimodal–transmodal and sensorimotor gradients, related to intralaminar connectivity and dynamic fMRI states.
ocar.future_work: They present the voxel-level scaffold as a route to intervention targets in a physiologically accessible species; causal perturbation is not demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: Most mouse brain maps average connections into large named regions. This study looks voxel by voxel and finds source-versus-sink hubs, a special role for neuromodulatory nuclei, and cortical gradients like those described in primates.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science Advances (2020), Coletta and colleagues give a voxel-level description of the directed mouse connectome unconstrained by atlas parcels. They report directional segregation of hubs into sinks and sources, structural communities that match known mouse resting-state fMRI networks, and neuromodulatory nuclei wired as connector hubs. Two superimposed cortical gradients (unimodal–transmodal and modality-specific sensorimotor) recapitulate a primate-like layout and are related to intralaminar connectivity and dynamic fMRI brain states. Resting-state BOLD acquisitions used TR/TE 1000/15 ms among other parameters listed in the methods extract.
summaries.advanced: The catalog lists the venue as bioRxiv, but the PDF is the Science Advances paper (DOI 10.1126/sciadv.abb7187). The selected text’s discussion was not captured (it runs into methods/references), so gradient and hub claims should be read as abstract- and introduction-level. Voxel analysis still depends on the underlying tracer-based directed connectome (Allen-style) and on fMRI preprocessing not fully detailed here. “Previously unappreciated” is an authorship framing.

plain_language_summary: Most mouse brain maps average connections into large named regions. This study looks voxel by voxel and finds source-versus-sink hubs, a special role for neuromodulatory nuclei, and cortical gradients like those described in primates.

ocar.opportunity: Because direct wiring diagrams are slow to obtain, many studies infer connectivity from simultaneously recorded activity, hoping sophisticated models will “explain away” correlations from common input.
ocar.challenge: In strongly recurrent circuits, unconnected but highly correlated neurons still attract inferred synapses when the inference model cannot match true dynamics—an inevitable mismatch in real data.
ocar.action: Das and Fiete, in Nature Neuroscience (2020; extract from the 2019 bioRxiv preprint), analyze inference algorithms including inverse Ising, l1-regularized logistic regression, and GLMs on activity from strongly coupled recurrent models, and test whether driving circuits far from equilibrium reduces bias.
ocar.resolution: Even with unlimited data from every cell, inferred connectivity is biased toward false connections between correlated but unconnected neurons. The error is a bias that does not shrink with more data, unlike variance at weak coupling. Sophisticated methods are often no better than inverse correlation in the strong-coupling regime. Pushing circuits out of equilibrium with strong noise or low-dimensional suppression is proposed as a partial remedy.
ocar.future_work: They argue that low-dimensional perturbations can disambiguate models, while full connectomics still leaves an inference step from structure to activity; both remain necessary.

summaries.beginner: People often try to guess which neurons are wired together just from how they fire. This paper shows that in tightly looped circuits those guesses stay systematically wrong even with huge amounts of data, unless you perturb the network out of its usual rhythm.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Neuroscience (2020), Das and Fiete show that activity-based connectivity inference is biased in strongly recurrent networks. The PDF extract is the January 2019 bioRxiv preprint of the same study. When weights are strong enough for memory-like persistence or substantial input amplification, explaining-away fails and unconnected but correlated neurons are assigned synapses. The error is bias, not sampling noise. Functional connectivity can still predict activity, but using it as a proxy for synapses can mislead developmental interpretation (e.g., ring versus sideband models). Non-equilibrium drive is suggested to ameliorate bias.
summaries.advanced: The extract is the preprint, whose title says “strongly coupled recurrent circuits” rather than the journal title “strongly recurrent networks”; authors and claims match the catalog paper. Quantitative bias magnitudes are not in this selected text. “Unlimited data from every cell” is a simulation idealization. Applicability to fMRI area-level inference is suggested, not demonstrated. Perturbation remedies are proposed rather than shown as a complete fix in the captured discussion.

plain_language_summary: People often try to guess which neurons are wired together just from how they fire. This paper shows that in tightly looped circuits those guesses stay systematically wrong even with huge amounts of data, unless you perturb the network out of its usual rhythm.

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila larva offers a compact, genetically tractable memory system whose mushroom body can be linked to behavior, single-cell manipulation, and an emerging complete CNS connectome.
ocar.challenge: Even in this much-studied insect memory network, connectivity classes, cross-hemisphere integration, and how dopaminergic inputs sign-switch with timing were incompletely known from light-level work.
ocar.action: Thum and Gerber, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), review larval mushroom-body connectomics together with functional and molecular memory results.
ocar.resolution: The connectome revealed that more than half of mushroom-body connection classes had escaped prior attention, and mapped circuitry that integrates higher-order sensory input, valence signals, and behavioral output neurons within and across hemispheres. Activating individual dopaminergic mushroom-body input neurons can reward or punish associated odors depending on relative timing. Larvae form molecularly dissociable short-term, long-term, and amnesia-resistant memories.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the larval mushroom body as a study case for a nuanced account of molecular function in a behaviorally meaningful memory network.

summaries.beginner: The fruit-fly larva has a small learning center that is now mapped at the synapse. This review explains how that wiring, plus timed dopamine signals, can make an odor feel rewarding or punishing, and how different kinds of memory can be pulled apart with genetics.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Thum and Gerber review connectomics and function of the larval Drosophila mushroom body. They emphasize genetic tractability, robust assays, single-cell manipulation, and an emerging complete CNS connectome in a ~10,000-neuron animal. The connectome showed that more than half of mushroom-body connection classes had been missed, and described integration of sensory, valence, and output pathways within and across hemispheres. Dopaminergic mushroom-body inputs can be rewarding or punishing depending on timing relative to odor, and larvae form molecularly dissociable short-term, long-term, and amnesia-resistant memories.
summaries.advanced: PDF mismatch: the extract is Yadav, Shinde, and Singh, Network Neuroscience (2025), “Brain rewiring during development: A comparative analysis of larval and adult Drosophila melanogaster connectomes,” not Thum and Gerber 2019. Summaries above use the catalog abstract only. Do not treat larval-versus-adult degree distributions, Weibull/power-law fits, or mushroom-body versus antennal-lobe cores from the PDF as results of this paper.

plain_language_summary: The fruit-fly larva has a small learning center that is now mapped at the synapse. This review explains how that wiring, plus timed dopamine signals, can make an odor feel rewarding or punishing, and how different kinds of memory can be pulled apart with genetics.

ocar.opportunity: Structural and functional connectomes span nanometers to centimeters and sub-milliseconds to years, so optical methods that combine speed, resolution, depth, and molecular contrast could map circuits that EM alone cannot follow in time.
ocar.challenge: No single microscope yet delivers high speed, high resolution, high contrast, deep penetration, large volumes, and molecular specificity together, and labeling, cell typing, and petabyte-scale analysis remain bottlenecks.
ocar.action: Gogoi, Keiser, Kao, and Chiang, in a 2019 book chapter in Advanced Optical Methods for Brain Imaging, survey optical modalities for high-throughput structural and functional brain imaging and the challenges of connectome-scale acquisition.
ocar.resolution: They review tools from light-sheet and related volumetric methods through examples such as SCAPE in behaving Drosophila. They note that a ~1 cm³ mouse brain might generate tens of petabytes at high resolution, and recall that reconstructing C. elegans (302 neurons; about 5000 chemical synapses, 2000 neuromuscular junctions, and 600 gap junctions) took almost 15 years with EM.
ocar.future_work: They envision new technologies over the coming decade while stressing that reconstruction and interpretation of mouse- or human-scale maps would still take far longer than imaging itself.

summaries.beginner: The brain has to be seen both up close (tiny synapses) and all at once (the whole organ), and both in a flash and over years. This chapter surveys optical microscopes meant to do that, and why the data still explode in size.
summaries.intermediate: In Advanced Optical Methods for Brain Imaging (Springer, 2019), Gogoi, Keiser, Kao, and Chiang review multiscale, multimodal optical imaging for connectomics. They frame required scales as nanometer-to-centimeter anatomy and sub-millisecond-to-year function, and survey high-throughput optical tools and remaining challenges in resolution, depth, and speed. The conclusion cites ~tens of petabytes as a possible load for a ~1 cm³ mouse brain and the ~15-year EM reconstruction of C. elegans (302 neurons; ~5000 chemical synapses, 2000 NMJs, 600 gap junctions) as a caution about interpretation time, not only acquisition.
summaries.advanced: This is a survey chapter, not a new instrument paper. Neuron counts for various species are cited from literature. SCAPE and other named methods are examples, not a head-to-head benchmark here. “Tens of petabytes” is an order-of-magnitude illustration. Journal field in the catalog is empty because this is a book chapter (DOI 10.1007/978-981-10-9020-2_1).

plain_language_summary: The brain has to be seen both up close (tiny synapses) and all at once (the whole organ), and both in a flash and over years. This chapter surveys optical microscopes meant to do that, and why the data still explode in size.

ocar.opportunity: Brain atlases and connectomes need not only connectivity but precise spatial coordinates tied to genome, proteome, transcriptome, and related maps—a program the authors call brainsmatics.
ocar.challenge: Network neuroscience and connectomics, they argue, under-emphasize affiliated spatial information, and no single instrument measures all desired molecular and morphological channels.
ocar.action: Shi, Guan, Chen, and Luo, in Photonics (2019), review optical-imaging contributions to tracing and surveying brain-wide spatial information and call for automation, standardization, and industrial-scale pipelines.
ocar.resolution: They argue optical imaging is the most appropriate route to a whole-brain connectome at consistent single-neuron resolution. Micro-optical sectioning tomography (MOST) morphology for one mouse brain is cited at about 10 terabits. They advocate integrating optics with RNA-seq and mass spectrometry and industrializing sample prep through reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: Suggested uses include disease comparison and brain-inspired algorithms; they explicitly request global interdisciplinary contribution.

summaries.beginner: This review coins “brainsmatics” for mapping the brain with careful 3D addresses, not just lists of connections. The authors argue that light microscopy is the practical way to see every neuron in a whole brain, and that the datasets will only work if labs share standard, automated pipelines.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Photonics (2019), Shi and colleagues define brainsmatics as brain-wide spatial informatics linking connectome, genome, proteome, transcriptome, and metabolome to coordinates. They review optical strategies for tracing and surveying, arguing optics uniquely offers consistent single-neuron whole-brain maps. They note MOST mouse-brain morphology at ~10 terabits, publication rates of brain-wide mesoscale imaging “no more than five per year since 2007,” and the need for automation, standardization, and industrialization analogous to genome centers.
summaries.advanced: “Brainsmatics” is a proposed banner, not an established field. MOST data-size and publication-rate figures are author-stated. No new atlas is produced here. Claims that optical imaging is “the most appropriate” for whole-brain single-neuron connectomes set aside EM synaptic resolution by design. Integration with RNA-seq and mass spectrometry is a requested platform, not a demonstrated instrument.

plain_language_summary: This review coins “brainsmatics” for mapping the brain with careful 3D addresses, not just lists of connections. The authors argue that light microscopy is the practical way to see every neuron in a whole brain, and that the datasets will only work if labs share standard, automated pipelines.

ocar.opportunity: Large-scale 3D ultrastructure at cellular scale was historically limited by difficult serial-section TEM and tomography, so a more reliable volume-EM method would widen cell-biology applications including connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Serial block-face SEM must balance membrane/vesicle resolution against field of view and subsequent image analysis.
ocar.action: Smith and Starborg, in Tissue & Cell (2019), review biological SBFSEM from a technical standpoint, emphasizing cellular applications and downstream analysis.
ocar.resolution: They describe SBFSEM, developed in 2004, as having increased reliability, availability, and throughput of 3DEM, resolving membranes and small vesicles while collecting large fields of view, and becoming a major tool in connectomics, cellular, and matrix biology.
ocar.future_work: The review points readers to image-analysis techniques after acquisition; it is a methods survey rather than a new instrument.

summaries.beginner: Serial block-face SEM lets biologists mill through a sample in the microscope and build 3D pictures of cells. This review explains how the method works, what it is good for—including brain wiring—and how the images are analyzed.
summaries.intermediate: In Tissue & Cell (2019), Smith and Starborg review serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBFSEM) as a 3DEM modality developed in 2004. They contrast it with serial-section TEM and electron tomography, noting improved reliability and throughput, resolution sufficient for membranes and small vesicles, and large fields of view. Applications cited include connectomics and cellular and matrix biology, with emphasis on technical practice and subsequent image analysis.
summaries.advanced: PDF mismatch: the extract is Chang, Li, Hong, Han, Chen and colleagues, BMC Biology (2023), “An intelligent workflow for sub-nanoscale 3D reconstruction of intact synapses from serial section electron tomography,” not Smith and Starborg 2019. Summaries above use the catalog abstract only. Do not treat serial-section ET, BP-Elastic alignment, 0.664 nm/voxel rat synapses, or the Chang workflow as results of this paper.

plain_language_summary: Serial block-face SEM lets biologists mill through a sample in the microscope and build 3D pictures of cells. This review explains how the method works, what it is good for—including brain wiring—and how the images are analyzed.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section SEM on tape can collect thousands of sections of varied size for connectomics and cell biology without requiring an in-microscope microtome.
ocar.challenge: As volumes grow from tens of microns to cubic millimeters, acquisition, alignment, staining, and handling become the bottlenecks even if cutting itself is relatively fast.
ocar.action: Baena, Schalek, Lichtman, and Terasaki, in Methods in Cell Biology (2019), describe practical ATUM procedures: block preparation, tape handling, post-treatment, mapping, imaging, and alignment.
ocar.resolution: They recap the Kasthuri et al. (2015) 50-micron cortical cube (~2000 sections at 30 nm, 3 nm/pixel) and note subsequent ~1000-fold larger reconstructions. They point to multi-beam SEM (61 or 91 beams), supercomputer alignment, and automated segmentation as responses to acquisition bottlenecks. The chapter is a hands-on protocol for labs adopting ATUM.
ocar.future_work: Fixation, cutting, collection, protein localization, and imaging are described as still under active improvement.

summaries.beginner: ATUM is a gadget that catches ultrathin slices on tape so a scanning electron microscope can photograph thousands of them. This chapter is a practical how-to, from preparing the block to lining the pictures up.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Methods in Cell Biology (2019), Baena, Schalek, Lichtman, and Terasaki detail Automated Tape-Collecting Ultramicrotome (ATUM) serial-section SEM. Sections are cut on a conventional ultramicrotome into a water boat, collected on moving tape, and imaged by SEM. They recount the Lichtman-lab origin and the Kasthuri et al. mouse cortex cube (~2000 sections, 30 nm, 3 nm/pixel) and the move toward cubic-millimeter volumes, where multi-beam SEM, HPC alignment, and automated segmentation address acquisition time. The extract also lists glow-discharge, carbon-coating, and post-stain supplies.
summaries.advanced: This is a protocol chapter; the selected PDF text’s later pages are equipment lists rather than new performance metrics. Volume and resolution numbers are historical (Kasthuri 2015), not a new dataset here. Multi-beam beam counts (61 or 91) are cited from Eberle et al. Protein-localization variants are referenced, not fully specified in the captured text.

plain_language_summary: ATUM is a gadget that catches ultrathin slices on tape so a scanning electron microscope can photograph thousands of them. This chapter is a practical how-to, from preparing the block to lining the pictures up.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian retinas contain more than 30 ganglion-cell types; mapping synaptic input to rare morphologies such as rabbit sparsely branched Class IV cells can show how feature selectivity is built.
ocar.challenge: Sparse, wide dendritic arbors resemble some amacrine cells, so identity and the mix of bipolar versus amacrine input were uncertain.
ocar.action: Bordt, Famiglietti, Marshak, and colleagues, in Visual Neuroscience (2019), partially reconstructed one SB3 ganglion cell in a rabbit retinal connectome from automated TEM and compared it with Golgi taxonomy.
ocar.resolution: Dendrites ramified in sublamina a and were always postsynaptic, supporting ganglion-cell identity. Bipolar cells provided 29% of input, typically one synapse per bipolar from multiple presumed OFF types, with infrequent reciprocal amacrine synapses at dyads. No crossover inhibition from narrow-field ON amacrine cells was apparent. Most amacrine input was from GABAergic axons and dendrites, likely from outside the classical receptive field. A similar cell was previously retrogradely labeled from rabbit LGN.
ocar.future_work: The soma region giving rise to the axon was not in the volume, so axonal identity is inferred from polarity and prior retrograde labeling rather than a traced axon in this cell.

summaries.beginner: A rarely discussed rabbit ganglion cell has long, thin dendrites that look a bit like an amacrine cell. Electron-microscope wiring shows it only receives synapses, gets about a third of them from bipolar cells, and lots of inhibitory input from far-reaching amacrine cells.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Visual Neuroscience (2019), Bordt and colleagues reconstruct a sparsely branched Class IV (SB3) ganglion cell in a rabbit ATEM connectome. The cell ramifies in IPL sublamina a, is exclusively postsynaptic, and receives 29% of synapses from bipolar cells—mid-range among previously studied rabbit ganglion cells—usually one synapse per bipolar from multiple presumed OFF types. Reciprocal amacrine synapses at dyads were infrequent; crossover from narrow-field ON amacrine cells was not seen. Most remaining input was GABAergic wide-field amacrine processes. Taxonomy is placed in Famiglietti’s four-class system, distinct from melanopsin SB1/SB2 (M1/M2) types.
summaries.advanced: n = 1 partially reconstructed cell. The 29% bipolar fraction is for this cell. The PDF OCR once reads “OLL bipolar cells”; the abstract and biology indicate OFF bipolars. Axon origin was not recovered. GABAergic identity of wide-field amacrine input is stated as likely, based on known wide-field properties, not new immunolabeling in this extract. ATEM connectome coverage limits completeness of the arbor.

plain_language_summary: A rarely discussed rabbit ganglion cell has long, thin dendrites that look a bit like an amacrine cell. Electron-microscope wiring shows it only receives synapses, gets about a third of them from bipolar cells, and lots of inhibitory input from far-reaching amacrine cells.

ocar.opportunity: ON parasol (magnocellular) ganglion cells respond to increments and to extra-classical motion; the wide-field amacrine cells that could carry those surround-like signals were incompletely identified in primate connectomes.
ocar.challenge: Most parasol input is amacrine, but which wide-field types contribute, and how that splits from glycinergic crossover, needed synapse-level counts.
ocar.action: Patterson, Bordt, Neitz, Marshak, and colleagues, in the Journal of Comparative Neurology (2020), reconstructed six neighboring ON parasol cells from a central macaque serial block-face SEM connectome and typed presynaptic wide-field amacrine cells.
ocar.resolution: On average, 21% of input was from bipolar cells and 17% from wide-field amacrine cells. Among 2818 identified input synapses, 78% (1733/2219) of inhibitory synapses were from narrow-field amacrine cells, matching the reported predominance of glycinergic crossover. Reconstructed wide-field types included semilunar Type 2 (polyaxonal, coupled to ON parasols) and wiry Type 2 (motion-sensitive). These inputs are proposed to heighten sensitivity to rapidly changing extra-classical stimuli.
ocar.future_work: Bipolar fractions varied across cells and across prior studies (baboon TEM ~20%; peripheral macaque 13%; some marmoset light-microscopy and parafoveal OFF parasol EM higher), so species and eccentricity remain open variables.

summaries.beginner: Parasol cells in the monkey eye are good at noticing motion. This wiring study finds that about a fifth of their synapses come from bipolar cells and another slice from long-range inhibitory cells that can report motion outside the cell’s classic receptive field.
summaries.intermediate: Published in the Journal of Comparative Neurology (2020; catalog year 2019), Patterson and colleagues reconstructed six ON parasol cells in a central macaque SBF-SEM volume and identified 2818 input synapses. Mean bipolar input was 21%; wide-field GABAergic amacrine cells provided 17% of all synapses (22% of amacrine synapses). Narrow-field amacrine cells accounted for 78% (1733/2219) of inhibitory synapses, consistent with glycinergic crossover physiology. Two wide-field types were identified: semilunar Type 2 and wiry Type 2. Data are viewed in Viking and SBFSEM-tools.
summaries.advanced: Six cells, central retina; bipolar fraction is an average with stated variability. Comparison percentages from other species and eccentricities are literature, not re-measured here. Wide-field “motion sensitivity” for wiry Type 2 is cited as a known physiological property. Coupling of semilunar Type 2 to ON parasols is from prior work plus identification here. Inhibitory transmitter (GABA vs glycine) is inferred from field type, not from new pharmacology in this anatomy paper.

plain_language_summary: Parasol cells in the monkey eye are good at noticing motion. This wiring study finds that about a fifth of their synapses come from bipolar cells and another slice from long-range inhibitory cells that can report motion outside the cell’s classic receptive field.

ocar.opportunity: Membrane detection in EM is the first step toward automated neuron reconstruction, but anisotropic, noisy, variable-thickness images still limit accuracy when labels are scarce.
ocar.challenge: Standard CNNs have limited receptive fields, and boundary maps are often blurry; fully supervised models also struggle with small EM training sets.
ocar.action: Chen, Zhu, Lu, and Luo, in Symmetry (2018), introduce ADDN: a conditional GAN whose segmentor is a densely dilated network, trained with adversarial loss plus dice loss, evaluated on ISBI 2012 EM and mouse piriform cortex.
ocar.resolution: They report state-of-the-art performance with less computation than several named baselines (FusionNet, CUMedVision, U-Net, PolyMTL, M2FCN), attributing gains to dense connections, dilated context, and reduced blur from the adversarial term. At test time only the segmentor is used.
ocar.future_work: They note small datasets and GPU memory from dense features as limitations, and suggest larger or transferred images, cheaper feature storage, alternative segmentor/discriminator designs, and a 3D extension.

summaries.beginner: Computers still struggle to outline neuron membranes in electron-microscope pictures. This paper trains a network that tries to fool a critic into thinking its outlines are human-drawn, and reports better, less blurry maps on two public EM sets.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Symmetry (2018), Chen and colleagues propose an adversarial densely dilated network (ADDN) for EM connectome segmentation. A densely dilated segmentor is trained against a discriminator in a cGAN, jointly optimizing adversarial and dice losses. They evaluate on the ISBI 2012 EM challenge and a mouse piriform cortex dataset, claiming state-of-the-art rand scores with lower compute than FusionNet, CUMedVision, U-Net, PolyMTL, and M2FCN. Discussion argues dense plus dilated context beats residual/skip designs that still need heavy post-processing.
summaries.advanced: “State-of-the-art” is the authors’ leaderboard claim on two datasets; numeric scores are not in the captured extract. Training data are acknowledged as small. GPU memory from dense intermediates is a stated limitation. Membrane segmentation is not full circuit reconstruction. Catalog tags include mouse; ISBI 2012 is Drosophila larva ventral nerve cord, so results span fly challenge data plus mouse piriform.

plain_language_summary: Computers still struggle to outline neuron membranes in electron-microscope pictures. This paper trains a network that tries to fool a critic into thinking its outlines are human-drawn, and reports better, less blurry maps on two public EM sets.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila central-complex models of heading and navigation have relied on presumed contacts from overlapping arbors in light microscopy, which may overestimate functional synapses.
ocar.challenge: The region is highly recurrent, genetically accessible, and involved in many behaviors, but cell-type connectivity needed direct functional tests.
ocar.action: Franconville, Beron, and Jayaraman, in eLife (2018), combined optogenetic stimulation, calcium imaging, and pharmacology to test 70 presynaptic-to-postsynaptic cell-type pairs, scoring connections against a null set of non-overlapping pairs.
ocar.resolution: They report many input pathways into the central complex but few output channels, sparser functional connectivity than light-level overlap suggested, and a potentially critical class of bottleneck interneurons. Data are released for interactive exploration on a website.
ocar.future_work: The matrix is cell-type resolution, not a full EM connectome; EM and behaviorally closed-loop tests are the implied next layer.

summaries.beginner: The fly’s central complex is a compass-like brain region whose wiring was mostly guessed from which cells’ branches overlap. This study actually stimulates one cell type and records another, and finds fewer working connections than the pictures suggested, with a few bottleneck cells in the middle.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2018), Franconville, Beron, and Jayaraman present a cell-type-resolution functional connectome of the Drosophila melanogaster central complex. Using simultaneous optogenetics, calcium imaging, and pharmacology, they tested 70 pre-to-post cell-type pairs. They find numerous CX inputs, few output channels, sparser connectivity than expected from light-microscopy overlap, and highlight bottleneck interneurons. Significance used Mahalanobis distance from non-overlapping control pairs in a space of scaled response integrals and across-fly correlation. All data are provided on an interactive website.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF text captures abstract, introduction, and methods statistics more than the named bottleneck cell types or the full matrix. “70 pairs” is a sampling of possible combinations, not an exhaustive census of CX cell types. Functional connectivity (calcium after stimulation, with pharmacology) is not anatomical synapse proof. Sparsity relative to light overlap depends on the overlap labeling and the control distribution. Website data are the intended companion to the paper.

plain_language_summary: The fly’s central complex is a compass-like brain region whose wiring was mostly guessed from which cells’ branches overlap. This study actually stimulates one cell type and records another, and finds fewer working connections than the pictures suggested, with a few bottleneck cells in the middle.

ocar.opportunity: S-OFF color signals in primates lacked a clear anatomical home, unlike the S-ON small-bistratified pathway, leaving open whether OFF midget cells carry short-wavelength information.
ocar.challenge: Prior EM in macaque suggested S cones contact OFF midget bipolars, but marmoset and some human observations questioned that path, and chromatic tuning of S-OFF midgets was unexplored.
ocar.action: Wool, Packer, Zaidi, and Dacey, in the Journal of Neuroscience (2019), used serial block-face EM in macaque parafovea and patch recordings in near-peripheral OFF midgets that combine L, M, and S input.
ocar.resolution: Every parafoveal S cone synapsed principally with a single OFF midget bipolar, which made a private-line connection to an OFF midget ganglion cell. Physiologically identified S-OFF midgets showed an S-cone spatial signature but heterogeneous color preferences spanning cardinal and noncardinal directions because L, M, and S weights vary across the receptive field. The OFF midget pathway is argued to be the major S-OFF conduit and a chromatically complex substrate beyond L-versus-M and S-versus-L+M axes.
ocar.future_work: Species differences (e.g., reported absence of the contact in marmoset) remain a caveat for generalizing to all primates or to human psychophysics.

summaries.beginner: Blue-OFF color signals in monkeys were a wiring mystery. This paper shows that in the fovea, each blue cone has a private OFF midget pathway, and that some midget cells mix blue, green, and red inputs in ways that are not just the textbook color axes.
summaries.intermediate: Published in the Journal of Neuroscience (2019; catalog year 2018), Wool and colleagues combine SBF-SEM in macaque parafovea with patch electrophysiology in near-peripheral OFF midget ganglion cells. Anatomically, every S cone contacted principally one OFF midget bipolar and then one OFF midget ganglion cell. Physiologically, S-OFF midgets have an S-cone spatial signature but heterogeneous 3D color tuning because L, M, and S weights vary. Preferred-vector plots separate clustered blue-ON cells from multimodal ON/OFF midget distributions, including nonopponent directions. The authors conclude the OFF midget pathway is the major primate S-OFF route.
summaries.advanced: Anatomy is parafoveal; physiology is near periphery, so the private-line EM result and the mixed-cone tuning are not from the same eccentricity. “Every S cone” refers to the reconstructed parafoveal sample, not the whole retina. Marmoset and human counter-citations are discussed as unresolved comparative issues. Cardinal-axis language is psychophysical; retinal encoding is argued to be richer, not that perception has been re-mapped here.

plain_language_summary: Blue-OFF color signals in monkeys were a wiring mystery. This paper shows that in the fovea, each blue cone has a private OFF midget pathway, and that some midget cells mix blue, green, and red inputs in ways that are not just the textbook color axes.

ocar.opportunity: Sparse tracing of labeled processes in large EM, X-ray, and confocal volumes often does not need dense segmentation, but supervised networks demand costly labels and can fail on new modalities.
ocar.challenge: Learning methods are error-prone and slow to retrain; global thresholds break under grayscale shifts and artifacts.
ocar.action: Shahbazi, Kinnison, Scheirer, and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2018), introduce FLoRIN, a learning-free sparse segmentation and reconstruction pipeline using neighborhood-dependent thresholding and structure-specific context, applied to mouse sSEM, SCoRe, and synchrotron µCT.
ocar.resolution: They report reconstructions of sufficient quality for preliminary biological study, orders-of-magnitude faster than supervised methods, and more robust to noise. On an SRB volume, 3D NDNT-based FLoRIN was a factor of 30 closer to ground truth than U-Net; 3D U-Net failed to produce meaningful results on sSEM APEX2-positive processes that FLoRIN recovered. New ALRB µCT and SCoRe volumes were segmented without prior annotations, including simultaneous cell and vasculature classes in X-ray data.
ocar.future_work: High contrast between microstructure classes can still require re-thresholding; the method is aimed at sparse, not dense, connectomes.

summaries.beginner: Machine-learning tracers often need lots of hand-drawn labels and still break on a new kind of microscope image. FLoRIN skips training, uses local brightness tricks, and the authors say it traces sparse labeled neurons in EM, X-ray, and confocal stacks much faster.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2018), Shahbazi and colleagues present Flexible Learning-free Reconstruction of Imaged Neural volumes (FLoRIN). It uses structure-specific context and neighborhood-dependent thresholding without training, on serial SEM of genetically labeled processes, spectral confocal reflectance, and synchrotron X-ray microtomography in mouse. They claim up to orders-of-magnitude speedups versus supervised models, robustness to noise and artifacts, a factor-of-30 closer match to SRB ground truth than U-Net, and successful APEX2 sSEM reconstructions where 3D U-Net failed. ALRB and SCoRe volumes were processed without manual training labels.
summaries.advanced: Comparisons are to U-Net on the authors’ volumes, not a full 2018 SOTA survey. “Factor of 30 closer” is their stated distance-to-GT ratio on SRB. Dense segmentation is explicitly out of scope. Multi-class success depends on contrast; they say a different threshold or window may be needed. Biological fidelity is described as sufficient for preliminary study, not as a proofread connectome.

plain_language_summary: Machine-learning tracers often need lots of hand-drawn labels and still break on a new kind of microscope image. FLoRIN skips training, uses local brightness tricks, and the authors say it traces sparse labeled neurons in EM, X-ray, and confocal stacks much faster.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans remains the only animal with a complete synaptic nervous-system map, so new whole-animal activity, perturbation, and modeling tools can ask how structure becomes behavior.
ocar.challenge: The wiring diagram does not by itself predict function: gap junctions, extrasynaptic peptides and monoamines, development, and dynamics all sit outside a static synapse list.
ocar.action: DiLoreto, Chute, Bryce, and Srinivasan review functional-connectomics technologies in C. elegans (catalog preprint 2018; PDF is the Journal of Developmental Biology 2019 version), covering imaging, optogenetics, sonogenetics, mutant analysis, and computational models including OpenWorm and dynome-style overlays.
ocar.resolution: They argue that combining experimental datasets with biophysical neuron models and behavioral quantification is required to interrogate local and global circuits. Developmental lineage is highlighted as shaping the final connectivity matrix. Sonogenetics is noted as an emerging non-invasive perturbation, with a 2016 FDA context for focused ultrasound in humans mentioned as a broader translational aside.
ocar.future_work: They expect structural and functional connectomics to expand with large brain initiatives and call for frameworks that span scales and systems.

summaries.beginner: We have a complete wiring diagram of the worm, but that still does not tell us how it behaves. This review walks through new ways to watch, tickle, and simulate the whole nervous system, including light, ultrasound, and computer models.
summaries.intermediate: The catalog record is a 2018 preprint titled “Functional Connectomics in C. elegans”; the PDF is the published review “Novel Technological Advances in Functional Connectomics in C. elegans” (Journal of Developmental Biology, 2019) by the same authors. They recap the 1986 EM connectome (hermaphrodite 302 neurons; male 385) as a prototype, stress that synapses plus gap junctions and extrasynaptic signaling still underdetermine behavior, and survey calcium imaging, optogenetics, sonogenetics, developmental studies, and modeling (OpenWorm; dynome overlays of dynamics on structure). The aim is a combined experimental–theoretical account of sensory-to-behavior processing.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not new mapping data. Neuron counts are standard citations. The human focused-ultrasound/FDA remark is analogical, not a C. elegans result. Extrasynaptic connectomes of peptides and monoamines are mentioned in the catalog abstract as recently described; the PDF emphasizes technological perturbation and modeling. Catalog journal field is empty (preprint DOI).

plain_language_summary: We have a complete wiring diagram of the worm, but that still does not tell us how it behaves. This review walks through new ways to watch, tickle, and simulate the whole nervous system, including light, ultrasound, and computer models.

ocar.opportunity: Laplacian embeddings of connectomes treat all nodes equally, so they can miss organization that is clearer when a biologically chosen cell class is emphasized.
ocar.challenge: Energy concentration (Slepian-like) and embedded-distance criteria pull in opposite directions; a stable compromise with user-chosen node weights is needed.
ocar.action: Petrović, Bolton, Preti, Liégeois, and Van De Ville, in Network Neuroscience (2018), derive a guided spectral embedding that jointly maximizes energy concentration and minimizes a modified embedded distance given an importance weighting, and apply it to the C. elegans structural connectome.
ocar.resolution: Opposite optimization goals yield a well-defined decomposition. Weighting sensory, inter-, or motor neurons tunes global versus local emphasis. Relative to Laplacian embedding, class-focused embeddings recovered known functional importance and added biological structure such as somatic position and involvement in low- versus high-order processing. Clustering modularity for class-focused assignments is illustrated against a null (e.g., values shown for inter-, moto-, and sensory-focused Q in a supplement figure).
ocar.future_work: The method is exemplified on C. elegans; transfer to larger connectomes is implied by the graph-signal-processing framing.

summaries.beginner: Usual map-making of the worm’s wiring treats every neuron as equally important. This method lets you spotlight sensory cells, or motor cells, and the resulting 2D maps line up better with where those cells sit and what they do.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Network Neuroscience (2018; extract includes an arXiv 2019 version), Petrović and colleagues introduce guided graph spectral embedding inspired by wavelets and Slepians. The criterion combines energy concentration with a modified embedded distance under a node-importance weighting, producing a stable spectrum because the two goals conflict. On the C. elegans structural connectome, focusing weights on sensory neurons, interneurons, or motoneurons yielded embeddings that confirmed known functional roles and, compared with Laplacian embedding, better distinguished somatic positions and low- versus high-order processing.
summaries.advanced: The selected text’s later pages are supplementary figures more than a full discussion of failure modes. Modularity Q values in a supplement (e.g., Q_inter ≈ 0.11, Q_moto ≈ 0.18, Q_sensory ≈ 0.18) are for a specific k-means clustering illustration, not a universal score. “More biological insights” is a qualitative claim versus Laplacian embedding. Application is one small connectome. Catalog dimension tags image-acquisition, but the work is spectral graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: Usual map-making of the worm’s wiring treats every neuron as equally important. This method lets you spotlight sensory cells, or motor cells, and the resulting 2D maps line up better with where those cells sit and what they do.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian brains organize into cell types whose long-range inputs and outputs define a mesoscale connectome between the DTI macroscale and synaptic microscale.
ocar.challenge: Building that map requires knowing cell-type composition per region and tracing anterograde and retrograde connections at population and single-cell resolution.
ocar.action: Zeng, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2018), reviews historical and contemporary tracing, imaging, and network-analysis approaches for mammalian mesoscale connectomes, written from the Allen Institute context.
ocar.resolution: The review distinguishes macroscale fiber-tract maps (e.g., DTI in living humans), mesoscale cell-type-to-region connectivity, and micro/nanoscale synapses. It surveys anterograde and retrograde tracers at population and single-cell levels and the imaging and graph analyses used to assemble brain-wide networks. The outlook expects acceleration from better cell-type taxonomies and reciprocal gains between cell typing and connectomics.
ocar.future_work: Zeng argues that uncovering principles for both cell types and mesoscale wiring is “within sight” given virus engineering, imaging, and genomics—an expectation, not a completed atlas in this article.

summaries.beginner: Brains can be mapped as big fiber highways, as cell-type-to-cell-type routes, or as every synapse. This review focuses on the middle scale and the tracing tools used to chart how each cell class sends and receives long-range connections.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2018), Hongkui Zeng reviews mesoscale connectomics: connections between neuronal types across brain regions. After distinguishing DTI-style macroscale, mesoscale, and synaptic microscale, the article surveys anterograde and retrograde tracing at population and single-cell levels plus imaging and network analysis for mammalian brains. The outlook ties progress to cell-type characterization, virus engineering, imaging, and genomics, with support from the Allen Institute and NIH grants U01MH105982 and U19MH114830.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/outlook, not a new connectivity matrix. The selected PDF extract is front matter plus a short outlook; named tracer systems and quantitative comparisons are not captured in the selected text. “Thousands of types” is an estimate. Human DTI is cited as the non-invasive macroscale route, distinct from the invasive mesoscale methods that dominate rodent work.

plain_language_summary: Brains can be mapped as big fiber highways, as cell-type-to-cell-type routes, or as every synapse. This review focuses on the middle scale and the tracing tools used to chart how each cell class sends and receives long-range connections.

ocar.opportunity: Linking function to synaptic structure in the same vertebrate brain is rarely possible; larval zebrafish are small and transparent enough for brain-wide two-photon imaging and subsequent EM of entire regions.
ocar.challenge: Registering calcium-imaged neurons to dense EM reconstructions requires specialized preparation, alignment, and proofreading tools.
ocar.action: Wanner and Vishwanathan, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), describe methods combining multiphoton microscopy with dense EM circuit reconstruction in larval zebrafish, with examples from olfactory bulb and hindbrain.
ocar.resolution: At 4–7 days post-fertilization the larva has about 100,000 neurons and is optically transparent. Dense olfactory-bulb reconstruction found most mitral cells largely uniglomerular while interneurons innervate multiple glomeruli according to glomerular identity, without specific input versus output glomeruli, implying strongly non-directional interglomerular interaction. They argue such questions need exhaustive joint connectivity and activity at single-neuron resolution.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a methods-and-lessons review pointing to EM protocol, segmentation, and citizen-science proofreading (EyeWire) as enabling pieces rather than a single new whole-brain map.

summaries.beginner: Baby zebrafish are see-through and small, so the same brain can be watched with a two-photon microscope and later taken apart in an electron microscope. This article explains how to do that and what the olfactory bulb’s wiring looked like when they tried.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), Wanner and Vishwanathan review combining two-photon calcium imaging with dense EM reconstruction in larval zebrafish (~100,000 neurons at 4–7 dpf). They cover tools for whole-region structure–function mapping. In the olfactory bulb, dense reconstruction showed largely uniglomerular mitral cells versus multi-glomerular interneurons whose innervation follows glomerular identity and lacks dedicated input/output glomeruli, suggesting non-directional interglomerular crosstalk that could aid odor-pattern decorrelation. Hindbrain work is attributed to Vishwanathan; olfactory bulb to Wanner.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods/perspective paper; OB findings cite Wanner et al. 2016 as well as work described here. “Most MCs are largely uniglomerular” is a qualitative majority statement. Joint activity-and-connectivity in the same cells is the recommended experiment, not fully quantified for every claim in this extract. EyeWire is acknowledged for hindbrain proofreading. Catalog dataset tag DS15 zebrafish matches the organism.

plain_language_summary: Baby zebrafish are see-through and small, so the same brain can be watched with a two-photon microscope and later taken apart in an electron microscope. This article explains how to do that and what the olfactory bulb’s wiring looked like when they tried.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans encodes over 300 neuropeptides that can signal beyond wired synapses, so identifying ligand–receptor pairs can add a wireless layer to the connectome-to-behavior program.
ocar.challenge: SEB-3 was an orphan secretin-family GPCR; which peptide, if any, modulates locomotion, arousal, and egg-laying through it was unknown.
ocar.action: Chew, Grundy, Brown, Beets, and Schafer, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), used reverse pharmacology to identify NLP-49 as a SEB-3 ligand and compared deletion and overexpression phenotypes.
ocar.resolution: seb-3 and nlp-49 deletion mutants caused similar locomotor-dynamic abnormalities, rescued by wild-type transgenes. Overexpressing NLP-49 in AVK interneurons heightened locomotor arousal in a seb-3-dependent way. Both mutants showed constitutive egg-laying in liquid and similarly altered egg-laying timing. The results provide in vivo evidence that NLP-49 acts through SEB-3 to control behavioral states.
ocar.future_work: They argue large-scale de-orphanization plus mutant phenotyping can build a multilayer neuropeptide connectome as a model for larger nervous systems.

summaries.beginner: Worms have a wireless chemical network of neuropeptides on top of their synapses. This study matches the peptide NLP-49 to the receptor SEB-3 and shows the pair helps control crawling, arousal, and egg-laying.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Philosophical Transactions B (2018) as part of the “Connectome to behaviour” issue, Chew and colleagues identify NLP-49 as a ligand of the orphan secretin GPCR SEB-3 by reverse pharmacology. High-content locomotion analysis found similar abnormalities in seb-3 and nlp-49 deletion mutants, reversed by overexpression of wild-type transgenes. NLP-49 overexpression in AVK raised locomotor arousal only if seb-3 was present. Both mutants laid eggs constitutively in liquid and changed egg-laying temporal structure similarly. The discussion links extrasynaptic peptide signaling to a wireless layer of the connectome.
summaries.advanced: Ligand assignment is reverse pharmacology plus matching mutant phenotypes, not a full binding-affinity table in this extract. Behavioral similarity of mutants is strong genetic evidence but not proof of exclusive pairing in every tissue. AVK overexpression is a gain-of-function manipulation. Comparisons to mammalian CRF/PDF systems are homology context; nematodes are described as having lost CRF. No new EM synapses are mapped.

plain_language_summary: Worms have a wireless chemical network of neuropeptides on top of their synapses. This study matches the peptide NLP-49 to the receptor SEB-3 and shows the pair helps control crawling, arousal, and egg-laying.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain calcium imaging in moving and immobilized C. elegans now shows what interneurons actually represent, testing whether the connectome’s feed-forward sensory hierarchy matches dynamics.
ocar.challenge: A sequential view—sensory neurons to first-layer interneurons to premotor hubs such as AVA—may be wrong if even first-layer cells are locked to instantaneous behavior.
ocar.action: Kaplan, Nichols, and Zimmer, in a Philosophical Transactions B (2018) perspective, synthesize whole-brain and freely moving Ca2+ imaging across studies, including their own prior work.
ocar.resolution: Most interneuron activity, including cells that receive direct sensory input, is tightly coupled to current behavior. They propose distributed, dynamical sensorimotor integration rather than segregated feed-forward pathways. AIB reversal-related transients can be as reliable as AVA by that criterion. In paralyzed, confined worms, about one-fourth of measured head-ganglion neurons show structured spontaneous-like activity aligned to motor-command states (forward, slowing, reversals, turns).
ocar.future_work: They discuss implications for experimental design (behavior as a confound and a signal) and note similar mixed selectivity in flies and rodents as possibly general.

summaries.beginner: Textbooks draw the worm’s brain as senses feeding forward into motor commands. Whole-brain imaging instead shows that even early interneurons fire with the animal’s current movement, so sensing and acting look mixed from the start.
