summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions B (2018), Kaplan, Nichols, and Zimmer reappraise C. elegans sensorimotor integration in light of whole-brain and freely moving calcium imaging. A common finding is that interneuron activity, including first-layer cells with sensory input, tracks instantaneous behavior, challenging a linear sensory-to-premotor hierarchy. They highlight AIB as reversal-coupled as strongly as AVA in some measures, and describe structured population dynamics in immobilized animals occupying motor-command manifolds (forward, slowing, multiple reversal states, dorsal/ventral turns). Similar mixed representations in Drosophila and rodents are offered as comparative context.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective synthesizing published imaging, including Kato et al. 2015 and related papers, not a new connectome. “About one-fourth” of measured head-ganglion neurons in paralyzed, microfluidic worms is a cited observation under confinement that may itself be arousing. Spontaneous versus tonic-sensory drive is explicitly uncertain. Reliability of AIB versus AVA is “by this criterion” (reversal coupling), not a full information-theoretic equality. Feed-forward anatomy remains true as wiring; the argument is about computation.

plain_language_summary: Textbooks draw the worm’s brain as senses feeding forward into motor commands. Whole-brain imaging instead shows that even early interneurons fire with the animal’s current movement, so sensing and acting look mixed from the start.

ocar.opportunity: EM and paired recordings map synapses reliably but not at high throughput, so a genetic proximity assay that lights up where two neurons actually meet would speed Drosophila circuit mapping.
ocar.challenge: Existing GRASP variants can fluoresce outside synapses or depend on activity (syb-GRASP), and they are not equally usable with all three fly binary expression systems.
ocar.action: Shearin, Quinn, Mackin, Macdonald, and Stowers, in the Journal of Neuroscience Methods (2018), fused split-GFP fragments to various pre- and postsynaptic proteins and selected t-GRASP pairings that concentrate reconstituted GFP at synaptic regions.
ocar.resolution: Paired pre- and post-t-GRASP constructs gave strong preferential synaptic signal in larval sensory neurons, larval NMJs, and adult photoreceptors with minimal false-positive signal in most driver pairs. Activity-independent t-GRASP was more synapse-specific than existing Drosophila GRASP methods. Stocks support pre- and post-t-GRASP in GAL4, LexA, and Q systems in either direction.
ocar.future_work: A minority of strong driver pairs still produced false positives, so the authors recommend corroboration (optogenetics plus calcium/ephys), STaR coincidence, dose-tunable repressors, and sparse drivers.

summaries.beginner: To see whether two fly neurons touch at synapses, researchers can split a green fluorescent protein across the two cells so it lights up only where the halves meet. t-GRASP aims that signal at real contact sites and works with all the common fly genetic driver systems.
summaries.intermediate: Published in the Journal of Neuroscience Methods (2018), Shearin and colleagues develop targeted GRASP (t-GRASP) by screening pre- and postsynaptic protein fusions for reconstituted GFP restricted to synaptic regions. In Drosophila larval sensory neurons, NMJs, and adult photoreceptors, dual targeting improved specificity versus existing GRASP tools and is activity-independent, unlike syb-GRASP. Transgenic stocks allow any two of GAL4, LexA, and Q drivers in either direction. Discussion warns that overexpression can mislocalize constructs and that t-GRASP positives should be corroborated.
summaries.advanced: “Minimal false-positive signal” is for the majority of tested pairs, not all; a small minority showed extrasynaptic signal attributed to overexpression. Coincidence with active zones (including STaR Brp-V5) is the operational synapse criterion. The method does not replace EM. Catalog tags include electron microscopy and larval dataset DS03, but this is a light-microscopy genetic tool paper.

plain_language_summary: To see whether two fly neurons touch at synapses, researchers can split a green fluorescent protein across the two cells so it lights up only where the halves meet. t-GRASP aims that signal at real contact sites and works with all the common fly genetic driver systems.

ocar.opportunity: Aging changes memory and sensation without massive neuron death, so dense EM of cortical neuropil can show how synapses themselves remodel.
ocar.challenge: Synapse counts can be biased by shrinkage and by incomplete sampling; volume-normalized and neurite-length-normalized measures are needed to claim true loss.
ocar.action: Calì, Knott, and colleagues, in PLoS ONE (2018), densely reconstructed axons, dendrites, and synapses from serial EM of layer 1 somatosensory cortex in adult versus aged mice (n = 3 volumes per group in the compartment analysis).
ocar.resolution: Excitatory synapse numbers fell but remaining synapses enlarged so synaptic surface per axon length and per neuropil volume stayed the same. Inhibitory synapses declined more, especially on spines, raising E/I balance. Correlations among spine volume, bouton volume, synaptic size, and docked vesicles were preserved. Mitochondrial volume fractions were unchanged (e.g., total adults 9.8 ± 0.76% versus aged 9.5 ± 0.37%). Adult axon length per synapse was 5.78 µm, close to a prior 5.69 µm estimate.
ocar.future_work: They interpret fewer, less transient connections plus larger remaining excitatory synapses as reduced plasticity with compensatory strengthening; causal links to behavior are not tested.

summaries.beginner: Old mouse cortex in this study has fewer synapses, but the ones that remain are bigger, so the total synaptic surface stays about the same. Inhibition drops more than excitation, which may make the remaining wiring stronger but less flexible.
summaries.intermediate: Published in PLoS ONE (2018), Calì and colleagues compare dense serial-EM reconstructions of layer 1 somatosensory neuropil in adult versus aged mice. Excitatory synapse loss is offset by larger synapses, conserving synaptic surface per unit axon length and per unit volume. Inhibitory synapses, especially on spines, decline more, increasing E/I ratio. Spine–bouton–synapse–docked-vesicle correlations persist. Mitochondrial occupancy did not differ significantly between groups. They argue the pattern indicates reduced plasticity with compensatory enhancement of remaining connections. Data are on Dryad.
summaries.advanced: n = 3 sub-volumes per age group for several occupancy tests; aging effects on behavior are not measured. Chemical fixation shrinkage is discussed; dense reconstruction is offered as a mitigation, not a perfect solution. “Transient connections” is an interpretive reading of fewer synapses plus conserved correlations, not a live-imaging result here. Layer 1 somatosensory cortex may not represent all cortical layers or regions.

plain_language_summary: Old mouse cortex in this study has fewer synapses, but the ones that remain are bigger, so the total synaptic surface stays about the same. Inhibition drops more than excitation, which may make the remaining wiring stronger but less flexible.
